study_identification.author_journal_year: Coupé et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2022
study_identification.title: Hippocampal-amygdalo-ventricular atrophy score: Alzheimer disease detection using normative and pathological lifespan models
study_identification.doi: Not explicitly stated in the extracted text

study_characteristics.study_objective: This study presents an innovative MRI-based method for Alzheimer disease (AD) detection and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) prognosis using lifespan trajectories of brain structures. The authors propose a novel Hippocampal-Amygdalo-Ventricular Atrophy score (HAVAs) based on normative lifespan models and AD lifespan models.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (C-MIND; NDAR; ABIDE; ICBM; IXI; OASIS; ADNI; and 7 other studies)

hc_age.answer: CN subjects ranged from 0.74 years (9 months) to 94 years across all datasets. Dataset-specific ages: C-MIND: mean 8.44 (0.74-18.86); NDAR: mean 12.39 (1.08-49.92); ABIDE: mean 17.53 (6.50-52.20); ICBM: mean 33.75 (18-80); IXI: mean 48.76 (20.0-86.2); OASIS: mean 45.34 (18-94); ADNI: mean 74.81 (60-90)

hc_sex.answer: Total CN across all datasets: F 1226 (46.2%), M 1429 (53.8%). Dataset-specific breakdown: C-MIND F129 M107; NDAR F174 M208; ABIDE F84 M408; ICBM F142 M152; IXI F307 M242; OASIS F187 M111; ADNI F203 M201

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: AssemblyNet preprocessing pipeline; image denoising (Manjón et al., 2010); inhomogeneity correction (Tustison et al., 2010); affine registration to MNI space; automatic QC RegQCNet (Denis de Senneville et al., 2020); intensity standardization (Manjón & Coupé, 2016); 250 DL models for segmentation; Neuromorphometrics protocol (132 structures)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Automatic QC RegQCNet (Denis de Senneville et al., 2020) and a visual assessment when failed after automatic QC. For all training subjects detected as failure by the automatic QC, visual assessment was performed by individually checking the input images and segmentations. If failure was confirmed by expert, the subject was removed from training dataset. Number of excluded subjects not explicitly stated.

modeling_method.answer: Polynomial lifespan models; z-score normalization to ICV; HAVAs computation

response_variable.answer: Brain volumes: hippocampus; amygdala; inferior lateral ventricle and HAVAs

predictor_effects.answer: Age is modeled as fixed effect using polynomial models (linear, quadratic, cubic). Model selection based on F-statistic (p<.05), T-statistic for coefficients (p<.05), and Bayesian Information Criterion.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some aspects of nuisance structure, specifically inter-subject variability through ICV normalization and inter-structure variability through z-score normalization. However, site/scanner effects are not explicitly modeled despite using multi-site data from 7 datasets. The paper does not discuss or model potential site effects, variance differences across sites, or other sources of systematic variability. The validation uses external datasets (AIBL, MIRIAD) which implicitly tests robustness to domain shift, and sensitivity analysis exchanges training/testing datasets, but there is no formal modeling of site as a covariate or hierarchical structure.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: To compensate for the inter-subject variability, we normalized all the structure volumes using the intracranial cavity volume (ICV). Moreover, in order to be able to combine several structures with different sizes, we performed z-score normalization of all the normalized volumes (in percentage of ICV). To do that, we first estimated the mean and the SD for each structures using all the CN subjects over the entire lifespan.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Volume normalization section, page showing lines 122-123

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study uses within-sample validation on the training ADNI dataset to perform initial screening of discriminant structures. Table 3 shows classification performance on the training ADNI dataset (404 CN vs. 332 AD) for 33 selected structures. This represents validation using non-independent data from the same domain, as the ADNI CN and AD subjects used for testing were also included in the training dataset.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: First, we selected all the multiscale brain areas (i.e., tissues, regional tissues, lobes, and structures) for which CN and AD models significantly diverged (i.e., confidence intervals stop overlapping at some point across lifespan). Thanks to this analysis, we obtained 33 areas. Using these 33 selected areas, we performed a screening to detect the most discriminant ones in terms of classification accuracy on the training ADNI dataset in order not to use testing data during method development.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Results section 3.1, lines showing selection of discriminant structures

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not perform validation on independent held-out data from the same domain. While ADNI data is used in training, the validation is performed entirely on external datasets (AIBL and MIRIAD for AD vs CN classification, and ADNI MCI subjects for prognosis). The ADNI MCI subjects used for testing represent a different clinical population (MCI) than the ADNI subjects used for training (CN and AD), so this does not constitute same-domain independent validation. There is no mention of train-test split or cross-validation within the training dataset for independent validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: To validate our model, we built a testing dataset based on two open access databases (AIBL and MIRIAD) to perform AD versus CN diagnosis task. Therefore, we validated the generalization capacity of our method and its robustness to domain shift. In addition, we used subjects with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from ADNI to estimate the capability of our models on prognosis task.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study validates the normative models on completely external datasets that were not used in training. Specifically, AIBL and MIRIAD datasets were used to test AD vs CN classification, representing different domain validation. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was conducted where training and testing datasets were completely swapped: AIBL, OASIS, and MIRIAD were used for training, and ADNI was used for testing. This demonstrates robust different-domain validation across multiple external cohorts.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: To validate our model, we built a testing dataset based on two open access databases (AIBL and MIRIAD) to perform AD versus CN diagnosis task. Therefore, we validated the generalization capacity of our method and its robustness to domain shift... Finally, in order to test the consistency of our findings, we changed training and testing datasets: AIBL, OASIS, and MIRIAD databases were used for training and ADNI was used for testing.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Testing dataset section 2.1.2 lines 94-96, and Sensitivity analysis section 2.1.3 lines 100-101

clinical_dataset.answer: AIBL for AD; MIRIAD for AD; ADNI for sMCI and pMCI

diseases_studied.answer: Alzheimer's Disease (AD); Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) - stable MCI (sMCI) and progressive MCI (pMCI)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score and distance from lifespan curves; HAVAs composite score based on distance to AD and CN models; Score normalized such that HAVAs > 50% indicates closer to AD model

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Classification performance metrics (BACC, SPE, SEN, AUC) used to evaluate diagnostic accuracy (AD vs CN) and prognostic capability (pMCI vs sMCI). Comparison with normative modeling (using 2σ threshold), classical ML methods (SVM with RBF kernel, LASSO logistic regression), and deep learning methods (ROI-based CNN, subject-based CNN, patch-based CNN from Wen et al. 2020). Sensitivity analysis with swapped training/testing datasets.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: HAVAs demonstrated very accurate AD detection (AUC ≥ 94% on external datasets AIBL and MIRIAD) and accurate discrimination between progressive and stable MCI (AUC = 78%), outperforming normative modeling, classical ML, and state-of-the-art deep learning methods.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: For diagnostic task (AD vs CN), HAVAs obtained 88% BACC and 94% AUC on AIBL (467 CN/82 AD), and 89% BACC and 96% AUC on MIRIAD (23 CN/46 AD). For prognosis task (pMCI vs sMCI), HAVAs achieved 73% BACC and 78% AUC on ADNI MCI cohort (255 sMCI/235 pMCI). HAVAs outperformed the second-best method by 3 percentage points for both diagnosis and prognosis. Individual structures performed as follows on AIBL: amygdala (80% BACC, 89% AUC), hippocampus (80% BACC, 88% AUC), inferior lateral ventricle (79% BACC, 89% AUC). Compared to state-of-the-art methods on AIBL AD vs CN: multimodel HAVAs (88% BACC) > ROI-based CNN (84%) > LASSO HAV (85%) > normative modeling (81%) > normative hippocampus (70%). Sensitivity analysis with swapped datasets (training on AIBL/OASIS/MIRIAD, testing on ADNI) yielded 87% BACC and 93% AUC, demonstrating robustness to training domain. The screening analysis of 33 brain areas showed that amygdala (AUC=88%), hippocampus (AUC=87%), and inferior lateral ventricle (AUC=82%) were the most discriminant structures on the training ADNI dataset. Models combining multiple structures (HAVAs) consistently outperformed single-structure models across all evaluation metrics and datasets.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The study does not explicitly model site/scanner effects despite using multi-site data, which could introduce systematic bias. The training dataset is heavily weighted toward older adults from ADNI, with younger CN subjects from different cohorts. The AD model assumes a smooth pathological trajectory by mixing AD patients (55-96 years) with young CN subjects (<55 years), which may not fully capture the complexity of AD progression. Sample sizes vary considerably across datasets (e.g., MIRIAD has only 23 CN subjects). The method requires accurate segmentation from AssemblyNet, making it dependent on preprocessing quality. The polynomial models (quadratic/cubic) may oversimplify complex lifespan trajectories. Validation on MCI prognosis uses subjects from ADNI (same source as training CN/AD), potentially reducing independence. The paper does not discuss potential confounders such as education, APOE status, or comorbidities.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Authors emphasize HAVAs simplicity makes it fully understandable and well-suited for clinical practice or pharmaceutical trials. The method uses very few parameters (<10) compared to CNN models (>10 million parameters), enabling better generalization and robustness to domain shift. Software package including AssemblyNet and HAVAs will be made freely available as downloadable Docker (https://github.com/volBrain/AssemblyNetAD) and online pipeline on volBrain platform (http://www.volbrain.net/). The authors note that while hippocampus volume is considered a hallmark of AD, amygdala volume provided better performance across all strategies when using single structures. HAVAs combines advantages of both normative modeling (easy interpretation) and classification approaches (accurate detection with pathology-specific decision boundary).

general_notes.general_notes: This paper presents an innovative approach combining normative modeling with pathological modeling, creating dual lifespan trajectories for both CN and AD populations. The key innovation is using distance to both models rather than just deviation from normal. The study performs comprehensive whole-brain screening across 132 structures, 5 lobes, 4 regional tissues, and 3 tissues, identifying 33 areas with significant CN-AD divergence. The method explicitly models pathological trajectories by mixing AD patients (55-96y) with young CN subjects (<55y), assuming neurodegeneration is a slow progressive process. Statistical rigor is demonstrated through F-statistics, T-statistics, and Bayesian Information Criterion for model selection. The full dataset list mentioned in training includes: C-MIND (N=236 CN), NDAR (N=382 CN), ABIDE (N=492 CN), ICBM (N=294 CN), IXI (N=549 CN), OASIS (N=298 CN, N=45 AD), ADNI (N=404 CN, N=332 AD). Validation datasets: AIBL (N=467 CN, N=82 AD), MIRIAD (N=23 CN, N=46 AD), ADNI MCI (N=255 sMCI, N=235 pMCI). The paper demonstrates that methods based on amygdala consistently provide higher accuracy than hippocampus-only models, challenging conventional focus on hippocampus as primary AD biomarker. The study uses same selection criteria as ClinicaDL (Wen et al., 2020) for defining clinical groups, enabling fair comparison with deep learning methods.
